learningObjectives.title: States of matter and the particle model
Separating mixtures: simple and fractional distillation
Separating mixtures: chromatography and Rf values

questions.q: What are the three states of matter?
questions.explain: The three states of matter described in the particle model are solid, liquid and gas.

questions.q: How are the particles arranged in a solid?
options: In a regular pattern, vibrating about fixed positions
Far apart and moving randomly at high speed
Close together but able to move past one another
questions.explain: In a solid the particles are packed in a regular arrangement and only vibrate about fixed positions.

questions.q: Which statement best describes the particles in a gas?
options: Far apart, moving quickly in random directions
Regularly arranged and vibrating in place
Close together, moving slowly past each other
Fixed in position with no movement at all
questions.explain: Gas particles are widely spaced and move rapidly in random directions with negligible forces between them.

questions.q: In which state do the particles have the most energy and are able to move most freely?
questions.explain: Particles in a gas have the greatest energy and move the most freely of the three states.

questions.q: Which property is typical of a liquid?
options: It has a fixed volume but takes the shape of its container
It has a fixed shape and a fixed volume
It fills the whole container and is easily compressed
It has no fixed volume and expands to fill any space
questions.explain: A liquid keeps a fixed volume because its particles stay close together, but it flows to take the shape of its container.

questions.q: What is the name of the change of state from solid to liquid?
questions.explain: The change from solid to liquid is called melting.

questions.q: What is the name of the change of state from gas to liquid?
questions.explain: The change from gas to liquid is called condensing (condensation).

questions.q: What is the name of the change of state from liquid to solid?
questions.explain: The change from liquid to solid is called freezing.

questions.q: Why are changes of state described as physical changes?
options: No new substances are made and the change can be reversed
New substances with new properties are always formed
Atoms are permanently destroyed during the change
The chemical formula of the substance changes
questions.explain: Changes of state only rearrange the same particles, so no new substance forms and the change is reversible.

questions.q: Why does the temperature stay constant while a pure solid is melting?
options: The energy supplied is used to overcome the forces between particles
The particles stop absorbing energy completely
Heat is being lost to the surroundings at the same rate
The particles begin to break apart into atoms
questions.explain: During melting the energy supplied weakens the forces between particles rather than raising the temperature.

questions.q: Compared with a mixture, how does a pure substance behave when heated?
options: It melts and boils at fixed, specific temperatures
It melts over a wide range of temperatures
It never changes state on heating
It boils at a lower temperature than any of its parts
questions.explain: A pure substance has sharp, fixed melting and boiling points, whereas a mixture melts and boils over a range.

questions.q: Which mixture is best separated by filtration?
options: An insoluble solid mixed with a liquid
A soluble solid dissolved in water
questions.explain: Filtration separates an insoluble solid from a liquid because the solid is trapped by the filter paper.

questions.q: Crystallisation is used to obtain which of the following?
options: A soluble solid from its solution
An insoluble solid from a liquid
A gas from a liquid mixture
questions.explain: Crystallisation recovers a soluble solid by evaporating solvent so the dissolved solid forms crystals.

questions.q: A student wants to obtain pure salt crystals from a salt solution. Which method should they use?
questions.explain: Salt is a soluble solid, so evaporating the water by crystallisation leaves salt crystals behind.

questions.q: To separate a mixture of sand and salt, the sand is first removed by adding water and then using which technique?
questions.explain: Salt dissolves in the water while sand stays insoluble, so filtration removes the sand as residue.

questions.q: Which technique is used to obtain pure water from a salt solution?
questions.explain: Simple distillation evaporates and then condenses the water, leaving the dissolved salt behind.

questions.q: Which method would best separate ethanol from a mixture of ethanol and water?
questions.explain: Ethanol and water are miscible liquids with different boiling points, so fractional distillation separates them.

questions.q: In fractional distillation of a liquid mixture, which component evaporates and is collected first?
options: The one with the lowest boiling point
The one with the highest boiling point
The one with the greatest volume
The one that is most dense
questions.explain: The liquid with the lowest boiling point boils off first and is collected before the others.

questions.q: What does paper chromatography separate?
options: Mixtures of soluble substances such as coloured dyes
questions.explain: Chromatography separates soluble substances by how far they travel with the solvent up the paper.

questions.q: Which equation is used to calculate an Rf value in chromatography?
options: Distance moved by substance ÷ distance moved by solvent
Distance moved by solvent ÷ distance moved by substance
Distance moved by substance × distance moved by solvent
Distance moved by solvent − distance moved by substance
questions.explain: Rf is the distance travelled by the spot divided by the distance travelled by the solvent front.

questions.q: A spot moves 3 cm while the solvent front moves 12 cm. What is its Rf value?
questions.explain: Rf = 3 ÷ 12 = 0.25, a value with no units between 0 and 1.
